clue.text: Poet, to right of centre, founder of cult

indicators.note: in an across entry, being to the right of something means coming after it, so the poet's word follows

parts.note: a hub is the centre of a wheel or of activity
a bard is a poet

explanation.surface: A literary figure with right-of-centre politics who started a cult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to right of centre' reads as politics; here it puts the poet after the hub. L. Ron Hubbard founded Scientology.
explanation.definitionFit: L. Ron Hubbard was the founder of Scientology, widely described as a cult.

clue.text: Hard work, energy and optimism

parts.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
op is short for opus, a work
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A recipe for success: hard graft, energy and a positive attitude.
explanation.definitionFit: Hope is a synonym of optimism, an expectation that things will turn out well.

clue.text: Melancholy, rude Conservative sportsman

definitions.meaning: the colour of the UK Conservative Party
a sportsman who has represented Oxford or Cambridge University earns a ...

explanation.surface: A gloomy, foul-mouthed Tory athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: Four definitions in a row. At Oxford and Cambridge a 'Blue' is someone who has played for the university against the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The one word covers sadness, smut, Tory politics and an Oxbridge sporting award.

clue.text: Better than expected, though not on course

definitions.text: Better than expected, though not on course

parts.words: Better than expected, though not on course
parts.note: the phrase means better than normal in everyday speech, but on a golf course scoring above the standard is worse, so the praise holds only off the course

explanation.surface: A result that beats expectations, though not on a golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf, par is the standard score and going over it is bad; everywhere else the same phrase means better than average.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means better than the normal standard, though golfers use the same words for a poor score.

clue.text: Airdrie district nurses like prunes?

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, so the two clue words cradle the letters of the answer

explanation.surface: Nurses in a Scottish town's district compared to prunes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nurses' looks like a noun, the subject of the sentence; it is a verb meaning holds. Airdrie is a town in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Prunes are plums that have been dried, so the question mark marks a definition by example.

clue.text: Demanding university hospital admit prince in poor health

indicators.note: a hospital admits a patient, taking them inside, so the prince goes in between the first two letters

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs
someone in poor health is ill

explanation.surface: A tough job for a university hospital: admitting a sick prince.
explanation.definitionFit: An uphill task is a demanding one, like climbing a slope.

clue.text: Posh, like Victoria?

definitions.meaning: upper-class, used of an affected accent
the Victoria is a variety of plum, so something like it is plum-like

explanation.surface: A query about whether someone named Victoria is upper-class, perhaps Victoria 'Posh Spice' Beckham.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Victoria Beckham, nicknamed Posh Spice; the second definition is the Victoria plum, a common British variety.
explanation.definitionFit: A plummy voice is a rich, upper-class one; plummy also means full of or like plums.

clue.text: Becoming callous and cool over time

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece over another means it sits above, so it comes first

parts.note: in means fashionable or cool
a duration is a length of time

explanation.surface: Someone growing hardened and cold as the years pass.
explanation.definitionFit: Induration is the hardening of skin or tissue, so the process of a callus forming.

clue.text: They comply, duffed up in cell

indicators.note: to duff up is to beat someone up, so these letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Prisoners who obey are beaten up in their cell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cell' suggests a prison; it is a white blood cell. 'duffed up' is British slang for beaten up.
explanation.definitionFit: A lymphocyte is a kind of white blood cell in the immune system.

clue.text: Plod round Luton with one of the underworld

indicators.note: the constable's two letters go round the rest, like an officer surrounding a suspect

parts.note: Plod is British slang for the police, so a police constable, PC
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A policeman walks around Luton with a gangland figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Luton is a town north of London. Pluto was god of the underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: Plutonic relates to Pluto, ruler of the underworld, and in geology to rock formed deep underground.

clue.text: Charlie recollecting words of hippopotamus?

indicators.note: read as re-collecting, calling the words back, so they are taken back to front

parts.note: the chorus of Flanders and Swann's Hippopotamus Song begins 'Mud, mud, glorious mud'

explanation.surface: Someone named Charlie remembers what a hippo said.
explanation.walkthrough: Flanders and Swann were a British comic singing duo; their hippo sings of mud. 'Charlie' is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A charlie is a fool, and a dumdum is a stupid person.

clue.text: Sexually excited male inhibited by nagging

indicators.note: inhibited suggests being held in check, so the male is held inside the nagging phrase

parts.note: to be on at someone is to nag them
he is a male pronoun

explanation.surface: A man's desire is dampened by someone nagging him.
explanation.definitionFit: On heat describes a female animal ready to mate, so sexually aroused.

clue.text: A number of marriages?

parts.note: the phrase seems to ask how many weddings, but a number is a piece of music, here the tune played at a wedding

explanation.surface: A question about how many times someone has married.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number' looks like a count; it is a musical piece, like Mendelssohn's or Wagner's played as the bride arrives or leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical number written for the procession at a wedding ceremony.

clue.text: Principled Greek, close to Syriza, agreed to be bound by resolution

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its last letter is used
being bound by something means being enclosed by it, so the agreeing word goes inside the abbreviation

parts.note: chimed, as in 'chimed with', means agreed

explanation.surface: A Greek with principles, near to the Syriza party, accepts a binding resolution.
explanation.walkthrough: Syriza was the left-wing Greek governing party. 'Principled' points to Archimedes' principle of buoyancy.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek mathematician is known for the buoyancy principle named after him.

clue.text: It lessens suffering of old man held by assassin

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father, one's old man
something held by a container is in it
an assassin is a killer

explanation.surface: Something easing the pain of a father taken hostage by a hitman.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the middle words as a statement: father in killer.
explanation.definitionFit: An analgesic, like aspirin, reduces pain.

clue.text: Gee, Sinatra excited these Republicans!

indicators.note: excited letters are stirred up and agitated into a new order

explanation.surface: A cry of how Frank Sinatra thrilled a group of conservatives.
explanation.walkthrough: Sinatra backed Ronald Reagan, so the surface fits the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Supporters of Ronald Reagan, a Republican US President, are named after him.

clue.text: Arachne broke drugs law — she took love potion

parts.note: Arachne is the setter, who refers to herself as I
dealing ecstasy breaks drugs law: sold E, with E for ecstasy

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to drug crimes, then names a woman who drank a potion.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Arachne broke drugs law' as the statement 'I sold E'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the legend of Tristan and Isolde she and Tristan drink a love potion.

clue.text: Twitch regularly observed

indicators.note: looking at a word at regular intervals picks out every other letter, starting from the first

explanation.surface: A twitch seen recurring.
explanation.walkthrough: The first, third and fifth letters of 'Twitch' give the answer, which is itself a twitch, often repeated.
explanation.definitionFit: A tic is an involuntary muscle spasm, often recurring.

clue.text: Lower limits removed, therefore start to dawdle

indicators.note: a word's limits are its ends, so its first and last letters are taken away
the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: With the lower limits gone, the pace turns slow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower' reads as 'less high', but it is a beast that lows, a cow; Hereford is an English cattle breed.
explanation.definitionFit: A cow lows, so a lower is a cow, and a Hereford is a breed of beef cattle.

clue.text: Female in the nude

indicators.note: the letters are found inside the two words that follow

explanation.surface: A woman shown naked.
explanation.definitionFit: A hen is a female bird, and in Scotland a woman.

clue.text: Methuselah, perhaps, voiced misgiving and lost nerve

parts.note: a methuselah is a large wine bottle, eight times standard size

indicators.note: spoken out loud, so the word is entered as it is pronounced, with its silent letter gone

parts.note: a doubt is a misgiving

explanation.surface: The biblical patriarch expressed doubts and lost his courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Methuselah' looks like the long-lived figure from the Bible; it is a large champagne bottle. Bottle is also British slang for nerve.
explanation.definitionFit: To bottle out is British slang for losing your courage and backing down.

clue.text: Greasy sandwiches start to nauseate mate

indicators.note: to sandwich is to put something in the middle, so the letter goes inside the other word

parts.note: fried food is greasy

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Fatty sandwiches begin to make a mate feel sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sandwiches' looks like a noun but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Mate is informal British for a pal or companion.

clue.text: Head waiter tolerated him behaving badly

indicators.note: the letters misbehave and refuse to stay in order

explanation.surface: The head waiter put up with an unruly customer.
explanation.definitionFit: The French title means master of the hotel, used for the head waiter in a restaurant.

clue.text: Public poverty after banks fail

indicators.note: a word's banks are its edge letters; once those go only the inner letters remain

explanation.surface: Widespread hardship follows a banking collapse.
explanation.definitionFit: Overt means openly shown, so public rather than hidden.

clue.text: Ma clipping lout twice

indicators.note: the clipped word is written two times
clipping trims off the end of the word, its last letter

parts.note: a yob is a lout

explanation.surface: A mother cuts a hooligan's hair on two occasions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ma' is not a mother: it is the surname of the cellist Yo-Yo Ma, defined by his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Yo-Yo Ma is a celebrated cellist, so his first name completes 'Ma'.

clue.text: Employs European aboard American naval vessel

indicators.note: a passenger aboard a ship is inside it, so the letter goes within

parts.note: USS, United States Ship, prefixes American navy ship names

explanation.surface: A US Navy ship takes on a European crew member.
explanation.definitionFit: To use something is to employ it, both verbs in the third person.

clue.text: Random old people in megalithic tomb

indicators.note: random arrangement means the letters are scrambled

parts.note: men can mean people in general

explanation.surface: Assorted elderly people found in a Stone Age burial site.
explanation.definitionFit: A dolmen is a prehistoric tomb of upright stones supporting a flat capstone.

clue.text: Groups of cyclists pootle around Nova Scotia

indicators.note: turned around, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: NS is the abbreviation for Nova Scotia, a Canadian province

explanation.surface: Cycling clubs ride gently about a Canadian province.
explanation.walkthrough: To pootle is British slang for to move along at a leisurely pace.
explanation.definitionFit: A peloton is the main bunch of riders in a cycle race.

clue.text: Son heard audible step

indicators.note: what can be heard is said out loud, so the letters are entered as they sound

parts.note: S is an abbreviation for son, and a case heard in court is tried

explanation.surface: A son listens to a footstep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' seems to start the sound device, but it is the court sense, tried; 'audible' is the sound signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A stride is a long step in walking.

clue.text: I used to be stupid and boring

indicators.note: letters that are stupid are muddled up, so these are rearranged

explanation.surface: A confession: I was once foolish and dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Tedious means dull and wearisome, the same as boring.
